title: Army Weekly Briefing
description: Army leadership, force design, modernization, contracts and the signal and network enterprise.
readFirst: Covers Nov. 9–20. New: Breaking Defense reported Nov. 19 that the Army Data Operations Center pilot now runs through Oct. 1, 2027, and that the center is still borrowing people from Aberdeen Proving Ground. ABC News reported Nov. 19 that Army Secretary Adam Telle postponed a controlled detonation of degraded lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant until Monday, Nov. 23. DefenseScoop reported Nov. 19 that the president nominated Lt. Gen. Patrick Frank for U.S. Northern Command and NORAD. No new NETCOM release and no new Army enterprise agreement dated Nov. 19–20 were found in Army CIO reporting, ESI, war.gov, Federal News Network, Breaking Defense, DefenseScoop, Nextgov, GovConWire, or vendor newsrooms. The Pegasystems award, W519TC-27-D-A019, is already known.

items.headline: Trump nominates Army Lt. Gen. Patrick Frank to lead NORTHCOM and NORAD
items.summary: DefenseScoop reported Nov. 19 that President Donald Trump nominated Army Lt. Gen. Patrick Frank to lead U.S. Northern Command and North American Aerospace Defense Command, and that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced the nomination Wednesday. DefenseScoop said Frank would be promoted to general if the Senate confirms him, and that he has been U.S. Central Command's deputy commander since June. He would replace Air Force Gen. Gregory Guillot, who took the dual-hatted command in February 2024. DefenseScoop said the commands are modernizing against cruise missiles, drone incursions, and hypersonic threats and are moving toward software-defined, artificial-intelligence-enabled defense networks.

items.headline: White House nominates Gen. LaNeve to be Army chief of staff
items.summary: Stars and Stripes reported Nov. 17 that the White House formally nominated Gen. Christopher LaNeve to be the Army's chief of staff, the job he has held in an acting capacity since Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth fired Gen. Randy George in April. Stars and Stripes said the Senate received the nomination Monday and referred it to the Senate Armed Services Committee, and that the White House the same day nominated Lt. Gen. Marcus Evans, director of the Army staff, to be vice chief. Breaking Defense reported that LaNeve said he has served 36 years, currently as vice chief, and that he is honored by the president's nomination. Stars and Stripes said it was not clear whether the Senate would act before a new Democratic majority is sworn in on Jan. 3, and that the White House has not nominated a permanent replacement for former Army Secretary Dan Driscoll.

items.headline: Sutten assumes command of CECOM and Aberdeen Proving Ground
items.summary: Army.mil reported Nov. 17 that Brig. Gen. Marne L. Sutten assumed command of the Communications-Electronics Command and the duties of Aberdeen Proving Ground senior commander at a ceremony on Nov. 16. The article said she leads a 9,000-person global command and is senior commander of a 28,000-person installation, and that she is the Army's command, control, communications, computers, cyber, intelligence, surveillance, reconnaissance, and medical materiel integrator. Lt. Gen. Gavin A. Lawrence, deputy commanding general and acting commander of Army Materiel Command, presided and said Sutten most recently directed network command, control, cyber communications systems integration on the G-6. Sutten said she is the 19th commander of CECOM.

items.headline: President nominates DEVCOM's Aberdeen commander and 35 other Army brigadiers
items.summary: The Department of War said Nov. 16 that Secretary Pete Hegseth announced the president has nominated 36 Army brigadier generals for appointment to major general. The list includes Brig. Gen. Robert G. Born, commanding general of Combat Capabilities Development Command at Aberdeen Proving Ground, Maryland, and Brig. Gen. Marne L. Sutten, who previously served as director of network command, control, cyber communications systems integration in the Office of the Deputy Chief of Staff, G-6. The release announces nominations, not Senate confirmations, and it does not say Sutten has assumed command of CECOM.

items.headline: Army introduces a reduced-range .50-caliber round and is testing it against drones
items.summary: The Army Combat Capabilities Development Command Armaments Center said Nov. 18 that it and the Portfolio Acquisition Executive for Agile Sustainment and Ammunition introduced a reduced-range .50-caliber round, the M1181 ball and the M1199 tracer, built so the bullet becomes unstable near Mach 1 and falls at less than half the distance of a standard round. The center said General Dynamics Ordnance and Tactical Systems designed the round the Army selected, and that soldiers can train on ranges sized for 7.62 mm ammunition. Small Caliber Munitions Competency Manager Kip Hess said use against small drones at close range is still being tested. Stars and Stripes reported Nov. 19 that the fiscal 2027 budget request includes nearly $5.4 million for about 520,000 reduced-range .50-caliber cartridges, and the center said reduced-range ball and tracer variants also exist for 6.8 mm and 7.62 mm.

items.headline: Army Test and Education Command is booking commercial firms onto six ranges
items.summary: Federal News Network reported Nov. 17 that Maj. Gen. Pat Gaydon, commanding general of Army Test and Education Command, said more than 120 companies have tested prototypes or are in the pipeline across six Army ranges since an initiative launched in August. The Army said 15 companies have completed tests on drones, counter-drone systems, missile interceptors, and long-range strike technologies, 14 are ready to proceed, and 93 are in the works, at Dugway Proving Ground, Yuma Proving Ground, Camp Grayling, Camp Atterbury and Muscatatuck, and a U.S.-run range in Morocco. Gaydon said the service is trying to bring firms in within 30 days of a request and now averages 33 days. Federal News Network said test officials from the other services met at Aberdeen Proving Ground in September, and that Brig. Gen. Mark Massaro said last month the Air Force is working with the Army on whether it could open its own ranges to commercial companies.

items.headline: Army Contracting Command opens a Manufacturing Rodeo for 400 one-way-attack drones
items.summary: DRONELIFE reported Nov. 16 that a Nov. 13 Army Contracting Command solicitation outlines a small-uncrewed-aircraft Manufacturing Rodeo pairing commercial manufacturers with the Army's organic industrial base. DRONELIFE said the effort covers Group 1 first-person-view one-way-attack and loitering-strike drones, with an initial batch of 400 flight-ready aircraft and 20 ground control stations at a maximum unit price of $3,000, and that the Army would supply batteries, motors, frames, and other specified equipment. The aircraft would compete at Drone Dominance Gauntlet III in March 2027, and successful participants could qualify for follow-on production of up to 10,000 aircraft at Army depots. DRONELIFE said a virtual industry briefing was scheduled for Nov. 16 and that the solicitation lists Nov. 20 as the overall response date, with an earlier deadline for initial solution briefs.

items.headline: Army awards General Dynamics a $332.5 million Stryker sustainment contract
items.summary: GovConWire reported Nov. 19 that the Department of War said Wednesday the Army awarded General Dynamics Land Systems, of Sterling Heights, Michigan, a $332.5 million contract for Stryker sustainment. GovConWire said the indefinite-delivery/indefinite-quantity award mixes cost-plus-fixed-fee, firm-fixed-price, and cost-no-fee pricing, and covers total package fielding, vehicle deprocessing, new-equipment training, and field-level maintenance. Army Contracting Command at Detroit Arsenal received three offers. GovConWire said work locations and funding will be set on each task order, and that work is scheduled to end Nov. 17, 2031.

items.headline: G-TEAD will award up to six OTAs after each Accelerated Capability Event
items.summary: Breaking Defense reported Nov. 16 that the Army's Global Tactical Edge Acquisition Directorate will award five to six other-transaction agreements after an Accelerated Capability Event, instead of one. Col. Christopher Hill, the director, told reporters Friday that the awards let small and medium-sized businesses that make it through a competition leave with an agreement, and that these agreements fund a 45-day operational assessment rather than a prototype. Breaking Defense said that assessment can then lead to one to three prototype agreements. The change started with an event in Hawaii, run with the Army's Pacific Command, on autonomous ground vehicles and command-and-control systems for sustainment and casualty evacuation, and Hill said the winners have not been named.

items.headline: Army extends the Data Operations Center pilot to Oct. 1, 2027
items.summary: Breaking Defense reported Nov. 19 that Chad Nash, deputy of the Army Data Operations Center, said at the AFCEA Data Forum that the pilot is extended from Oct. 1, 2026, to Oct. 1, 2027 so the Army can keep measuring the volume of data problems it is clearing. Breaking Defense said the center was established in April as a 180-day pilot and help desk for formations, especially at the tactical edge, that could not get to their data. Col. Reginald Evans, director of the Command and Control Future Capability Directorate and the center, said the Army still would not have enough people to fill permanent billets and is relying on personnel borrowed from other organizations at Aberdeen Proving Ground. Nash said problems that took about two months at the start are now being solved in days, and that senior leaders will decide after the extension whether the center becomes permanent.

items.headline: 11th Airborne keeps a digital mission-command link on a no-stop flight to Hawaii
items.summary: The Department of War reported Nov. 18 that paratroopers from the 11th Airborne Division flew from Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson, Alaska, rigged in flight, and jumped into Hawaii during Joint Pacific Multinational Readiness Center Rotation 27-01. Col. Matthew Adamczyk, the division's deputy commanding officer for operations, said the division monitored the battlefield from the aircraft and kept a digital link with I Corps and the joint force. The department said the flight applied the Army's operational guidance "How the Army Fights," and that I Corps coordinated space, cyber, and electronic assets while the 25th Infantry Division struck simulated air defenses before the jump. It said the rotation includes about 10,000 personnel, and that the paratroopers will return to Alaska for another airborne assault before a February rotation.

items.headline: Army postpones an Iowa lead-azide detonation until Monday
items.summary: ABC News reported Nov. 19 that Army Secretary Adam Telle said he directed Army Materiel Command to postpone a controlled detonation at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown from Friday until Monday, Nov. 23, and that he called public safety the Army's top priority. ABC News said Army Sustainment Command spokesperson Justine Barati put the material at 68 barrels, approximately 9,700 pounds of degraded lead azide, and that Telle said Monday is the latest moment before a forecasted temperature drop that could further destabilize it. The Army told ABC News that destroying the material in place is the only responsible option because packing and transporting it risks an accidental detonation. ABC News said the Iowa Environmental Council and the Sierra Club asked a federal court to halt the Environmental Protection Agency permit, and that Sen. Chuck Grassley said the delay is meant to further educate the public.
